summary: This paper presents an anatomy-aware multimodal framework for predicting the T-stage of laryngopharyngeal cancer using 3D CT scans and paired radiology reports. The framework constructs an Anatomy-Structured Organ Graph (AOG) to model spatial relationships, aligns organ features with textual descriptions via Organ-Anchored Cross-Modal Alignment (OCA), and refines the graph using Report-Enhanced Graph-Refinement (REG). Evaluated on a multi-center cohort of 656 patients, the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art unimodal and multimodal baselines in both binary and three-class staging tasks.

Abstract— Accurate T-staging is crucial for guiding personalized treatment strategies for laryngopharyngeal cancer. However, current clinical practice relies on invasive
biopsy procedures, whereas CT-based staging remains
challenging due to the complex patterns of tumor invasion. Recent computer-aided approaches face two key
challenges: 1) Structural relationship modeling: existing
methods underrepresent anatomically structured patterns
of tumor invasion, as they either process whole CT volumes without tumor-specific anatomical constraints or rely
on labor-intensive tumor segmentation. 2) Fine-grained
cross-modal alignment: while radiology reports contain
organ-specific invasion details, current methods that apply global feature fusion struggle to accurately align individual anatomical structures with their corresponding
textual descriptions. To address these issues, we propose
an anatomy-aware multimodal framework that integrates
organ-level CT context and radiology reports into a unified representation for laryngopharyngeal T-staging. The
framework first constructs an Anatomy-Structured Organ
Graph (AOG) that captures invasion patterns between primary sites and surrounding organs, then performs OrganAnchored Cross-Modal Alignment (OCA) so that each organ
node aggregates textual evidence from the radiology report, and finally refines this graph representation by injecting organ-specific invasion cues extracted from the report
via Report-Enhanced Graph-Refinement (REG), yielding a
multimodal organ graph that combines spatial and textual evidence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the

II. R ELATED W ORK
A. T-staging
T-staging is a key component of cancer staging, describing
the size, extent, and invasion depth of the primary tumor.
Accurate staging is vital for diagnosis, treatment planning,
and prognosis evaluation. CT, MRI, PET and endoscopic
ultrasound are widely applied in clinical practice. Recent
advances in deep learning have spurred interest in automating
T-staging of cancers based on various imaging modalities.
For rectal cancer, Han et al. [16] employ a convolutional
neural network (CNN) to predict T-stage from CT, capturing
subtle infiltration cues. Zhang et al. [17] propose a tensor
graph network exploiting spatial–structural information for
improved segmentation-based staging. Dong et al. [18] develop
a cross-domain mutual-assistance framework for nasopharyngeal cancer, and further introduced interpretable dual-branch
networks (IPNet) for endoscopic ultrasound-based rectal Tstaging. In prostate cancer, Ogino et al. [19] present a feature
space transfer model using MRI to address domain adaptation
and enhance robustness. For head and neck cancers, Gilbert
et al. [20] compare standard and dedicated laryngopharyngeal CT for staging accuracy, while Kuno et al. [9] review
CT, MRI, and dual-energy CT applications. Liu et al. [11]
build a radiomics-based classifier to distinguish T2 from T3
in laryngopharyngeal cancer (LHSCC), and Chen et al. [6]
achieve improved laryngopharyngeal cancer staging via multimodal fusion of radiomics and deep learning using CT.
These laryngopharyngeal and head-and-neck staging studies,
however, are single-center, limited in scale (118–319 patients),
and rely on imaging features alone without exploiting paired
radiology reports. Despite the progress, laryngopharyngeal
cancer staging remains challenging due to complex invasion
patterns, limited CT resolution and contrast, and insufficient
structural modeling in current algorithms. We address these
gaps with a multimodal framework that integrates anatomical
relationship modeling and textual evidence, aiming to enhance
fine-grained invasion characterization and T-staging accuracy.
B. Multi-modal Learning
Multi-modal learning leverages complementary information
from diverse data modalities and has shown strong potential
in clinical diagnosis and medical image analysis [21], [22].
By integrating medical images with textual reports, such
models capture richer semantic representations, improving
both diagnostic accuracy and interpretability [23], [24]. Recent
studies have explored vision–language integration for medical
imaging. TP-DRSeg [25] injects medical prior knowledge

B. Experimental Setup
1) Implementation Details: All experiments are conducted
using PyTorch [41] on an NVIDIA H20 GPU. For data
preprocessing, all CT volumes are resampled to an isotropic
spacing of 1mm3 and resized to a unified spatial dimension
of 128×128×128. The intensity values are normalized to the
range [0, 1], with Hounsfield Unit normalization applied using
a window center of 50 and a window width of 450 to enhance
the visibility of soft tissues in clinical settings. We train our
model with a batch size of 8 using the Adam optimizer. The
learning rate starts at 1×10−6 and decays to 1×10−7 following
a cosine decay schedule, with a weight decay of 1 × 10−5 .
Organ masks for all four cohorts are produced by the same
publicly available pre-trained segmentation model (Continual
Segment [15], a single unified model covering 143 whole-body
organs in CT), applied without any site-specific fine-tuning or
adaptation.
2) Evaluation Criteria: We evaluate model performance using Accuracy and Macro F1-score. Accuracy reflects the
proportion of correct predictions, F1-score balances precision

C. Comparison to State-of-the-Arts
We compare the proposed method with image-based classification approaches, such as SwinViT [37], VDPF [38],
MRSN [39], and several state-of-the-art multimodal learning
methods (CPAM [5], TGCAM [2], MMBCD [1], LViT [4],
MMI [3]). The results are summarized in Table II. Our method
demonstrates superior performance across all experimental
settings. In the binary classification task (Early T1–T2 vs. Late
T3–T4), our method achieves the highest performance on both
internal and external test sets. For internal testing, we achieve
an F1 score of 80.83% and accuracy of 81.53%, surpassing the
second-best method MMI [3] (77.59% F1 score and 78.57%
accuracy). On the external test set, our method maintains its
leading position with an F1 score of 76.46% and accuracy
of 76.50%, outperforming TGCAM [2] (74.09% F1 score
and 74.38% accuracy) by a significant margin. For the more
challenging three-class classification task (T1, T2, T3–T4),
our method also achieves consistent superior performance.
On the internal test set, we achieve an F1 score of 61.43%
and accuracy of 63.33%, showing notable improvements over
MMBCD [1] (58.44% F1 score and 61.14% accuracy). The
advantage is even more prominent on the external test set,
where our method achieves an F1 score of 60.27% and
accuracy of 63.78%, significantly outperforming the second
best method by a large margin of 8.73% F1 score and 7.78%
accuracy.

1) Effectiveness of Individual Components: We conduct
comprehensive ablation studies to evaluate the contribution
of each key component in our framework. As shown in
Table IV, we systematically analyze different combinations
of the three main modules: Anatomy-Structured Organ Graph
(AOG), Organ-Anchored Cross-Modal Alignment (OCA),
and Report-Enhanced Graph-Refinement (REG). The baseline model, which directly processes the whole CT volume
for prediction without any anatomical guidance or textual
information, achieves only 58.76% and 39.16% macro F1scores in binary and three-class settings, respectively. Adding
AOG substantially improves the performance (77.96% and
52.80% F1-scores), demonstrating that explicitly modeling

When applying the OCA module alone, the performance

observe further performance gains (81.63% and 61.52% F1scores), suggesting that anatomical structure and textual evidence complement each other. Finally, incorporating REG on
top of both AOG and OCA yields the best overall performance,
with macro F1-scores of 83.96% and 64.53% in binary and

Report–T-stage Independence. Under AJCC 8th edition criteria, thyroid cartilage invasion is a hallmark of advanced
T-stage in laryngopharyngeal cancer. To examine whether
invasion descriptions in reports could implicitly encode Tstage, we analyzed thyroid cartilage-related descriptions across
the 439 FUZH reports (Table IX). Of 147 reports with positive
invasion descriptions, 45 (30.6%) are from pathologically
confirmed early-stage (T1–T2) patients; conversely, among
172 advanced-stage (T3–T4) patients, 70 (40.7%) lack any
positive description. This is because invasion descriptions reflect CT-visible findings — an imaging observation rather than
a pathological diagnosis — and CT alone cannot determine
whether true cartilage invasion has occurred [7], [14], [20].
This substantial discordance confirms that invasion descriptions do not encode T-stage, ruling out information circularity
in our framework.
Report Quality and Cross-Institutional Robustness. All
radiology reports in our study are routine clinical documents,
not research-curated texts. The 439 FUZH training reports
vary in detail and phrasing across radiologists while sharing
a common reporting template, and the three external test
sets (CGMH, EENT, TCGA) follow their own institutional
conventions. Among the three modules, AOG operates entirely
on CT features and is report-independent; OCA aligns reports
to organs through learned cross-attention rather than keyword
matching; and REG extracts structural invasion relations from
report text that are typically documented even in brief reports
when clinically relevant. The stable cross-institutional performance (Table II) is consistent with the design accommodating
reporting variation in practice.
A controlled report-detail perturbation experiment
(Fig. 5(b)) provides direct support for this: keeping the
same images and the frozen model while rewriting each
report to be less- or more-detailed changes macro-F1 by at

most 1.7 points and accuracy by at most 1.2 points.
Clinical Deployment Considerations. Several practical challenges should be considered for clinical deployment. First,
the framework depends on a pre-trained organ segmentation
model, whose performance may vary across imaging protocols
and scanner vendors; validating or fine-tuning the segmentation model on site-specific data is advisable before deployment. Second, differences in reporting terminology and detail
across institutions may affect the OCA and REG modules,
though our cross-institutional evaluation suggests the learned
cross-attention mechanism accommodates such variation reasonably well. Third, prospective validation on independent
cohorts with different disease distributions is essential before
integration into clinical decision-support workflows.
VI. C ONCLUSION
In this work, we introduced an anatomy-structured multimodal framework for laryngopharyngeal cancer T-staging that
integrates CT volumes and paired radiology reports. By explicitly modeling anatomical topology through the AnatomyStructured Organ Graph (AOG), performing organ-level crossmodal alignment via the Organ-Anchored Cross-Modal Alignment (OCA) module, and incorporating structured clinical invasion knowledge using the Report-Enhanced GraphRefinement (REG) module, our method effectively captures
organ-specific invasion patterns and their textual evidence. Extensive experiments on the largest curated laryngopharyngeal
cancer T-staging dataset, as well as on public benchmarks,
demonstrated that our proposed framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art unimodal and multimodal baselines
in both binary and multi-class staging tasks, achieving notable gains over radiologist assessments. Beyond performance,
our framework offers improved interpretability by aligning
decision-making with clinically meaningful invasion pathways, thereby enhancing its potential for real-world adoption.
Future work will explore extending the proposed topologyaware design to other head-and-neck and thoracic malignancies, as well as integrating longitudinal imaging and follow-up
reports to enable dynamic tumor progression modeling.

Table VII shows the comparison results of our method and
two radiologists on an external test set. For this evaluation, we
randomly selected 20 samples from each class, comprising 80
samples in total for the comparison. The proposed method
demonstrates competitive performance with the radiologists in
both experimental settings. In the Early vs Late classification,
our method achieves an F1 score of 76.25% and accuracy of

76.25%, performing comparably to Radiologists 1 and 2, who
achieve F1 scores of 76.16% and 74.98%, and accuracies of
76.25% and 75.00%, respectively. In the T1, T2, Late (T3–T4)
classification, our method achieves an F1 score of 59.71% and
an accuracy of 62.50%, outperforming both radiologists by at
least 6.08% in F1 score and 2.50% in accuracy. These results
confirm the effectiveness of our method in predicting laryngopharyngeal cancer T-staging, demonstrating performance on
par with or exceeding experienced radiologists. The three representative cases in Fig. 7 demonstrate that, despite potential
errors by experienced clinicians, our model correctly performs
the T-staging task, showing strong precision and robustness.
We analyzed the 16 misclassified cases (out of 88 test
samples) in Fold 1 and identified two dominant failure patterns
inherently linked to the limitations of CT-based invasion
assessment. Over-staging (9/16 cases, 56%): the model predicted T3–T4 for pathologically confirmed T1–T2 cases. In
7 of these 9 cases, the radiology report explicitly described
cartilage invasion that was not confirmed by pathological examination, reflecting CT’s known limitation in distinguishing
tumor contact from true cartilage invasion [7], [14]. Understaging (7/16 cases, 44%): the model predicted T1–T2 for
pathologically confirmed T3–T4 cases. In 5 of these 7 cases,
the report contained no invasion description or explicitly stated
“no evidence of invasion,” despite pathological confirmation.
These complementary failure modes highlight an inherent
challenge: CT-based assessment can both over-estimate and
under-estimate invasion relative to pathological ground truth.
Three representative failure cases are shown in Fig. 7.

examine the misclassified cases in the shared representation
space, quantifying the OCA cross-attention mass that the
potentially-invaded organ nodes (esophagus, thyroid gland,
trachea, oral cavity) place on invasion-related report tokens
(Table VIII). On correctly classified cases the alignment
behaves as intended, with low values for true early-stage
(0.058) and high values for true advanced-stage cases (0.105).

reports genuinely contain invasion descriptions that are CTderived false positives (cf. the cartilage discordance in Table IX), which the cross-modal fusion faithfully incorporates,

early-stage cases (0.058), consistent with these being CT false
negatives in which the report records no positive invasion

Report–T-stage Independence. Under AJCC 8th edition criteria, thyroid cartilage invasion is a hallmark of advanced
T-stage in laryngopharyngeal cancer. To examine whether
invasion descriptions in reports could implicitly encode Tstage, we analyzed thyroid cartilage-related descriptions across
the 439 FUZH reports (Table IX). Of 147 reports with positive
invasion descriptions, 45 (30.6%) are from pathologically
confirmed early-stage (T1–T2) patients; conversely, among
172 advanced-stage (T3–T4) patients, 70 (40.7%) lack any
positive description. This is because invasion descriptions reflect CT-visible findings — an imaging observation rather than
a pathological diagnosis — and CT alone cannot determine
whether true cartilage invasion has occurred [7], [14], [20].
This substantial discordance confirms that invasion descriptions do not encode T-stage, ruling out information circularity
in our framework.
